items.title: Nat Hentoff interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007
items.q: I once told Beethoven someday his music would be recorded.

ctx.x: Yeah, as you said, there’s a lot of longevity here, you’ve been around for so long.

I was amazed, I went back to my alma matter, Boston Latin School. And by the way, that was the one mistake, factual, that Sandra Day O’Connor made in one of her opinions. She said public education in America started in the eighteenth century. Boston Latin School was founded in 1636. And that changed my life, the six years there. This was the depression, most of us were poor. The rich kids went to Exeter or Andover. And the teachers, who were called masters, didn’t want to hear of any problems at home, whether we…
Yeah, you’d have been expelled for that.

items.title: Hentoff Nat — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I also told Beethoven someday his music would be recorded.

ctx.x: Your years there were from what grade?

I stayed there from seventh grade through graduation. By the way, I came back there a few years ago, and to my great surprise, there was a functioning jazz band, which was totally out of possibility when I was a kid. They have a very good bandmaster there. The kids – of course the front line was different from anything we had. There was a girl, a black player, an Asian player, some white kids. They were playing Ellington’s Things ain’t what they used to be, which was an apt tune for the time. At the end of it I…
In a sense in a very jazz-improvisatory kind of way, being open to the moment.
